prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

﻿When it is cold it stinks, and not till then. The seasonable or more rabid heats Of love and summer in some other cities Unseal the all too human: not in his. When it is cold it stinks, but not before; Smells to high heaven then most creaturely When it is cold. It stinks, but not before His freezing eye has done its best to maim, To amputate limbs, livelihood and name, Abstracting life beyond all likelihood. When it is cold it stinks, and not till then Can it be fragrant. On canal and street, Colder and colder, Murphy to Molloy, The weather hardens round the Idiot Boy, The gleeful hero of the long retreat. When he is cold he stinks, but not before, This living corpse. The existential weather Smells out in these abortive minims, men Who barely living therefore altogether Live till they die; and sweetly smell till then.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: When, The, Unseal

outputs.L1:
When it is cold, it stinks—and not till then.  
The seasonal, more rabid heats  
Of love and summer in other cities  
Unseal the all-too-human; not in his.  
When it is cold, it stinks, but not before;  
Then it smells to high heaven, most creaturely,  
When it is cold. It stinks, but not before  
His freezing eye has done its utmost to maim,  
To amputate limbs, livelihood, and name,  
Abstracting life beyond all likelihood.  

When it is cold, it stinks—and not till then  
Can it be fragrant. On canal and street,  
Colder and colder, Murphy to Molloy,  
The weather hardens round the Idiot Boy,  
The gleeful hero of the long retreat.  

When he is cold, he stinks, but not before,  
This living corpse. The existential weather  
Smells out in these abortive minims: men  
Who, barely living, therefore altogether  
Live till they die—and sweetly smell till then.

outputs.L3:
The poem suggests that coldness has the power to expose a hidden stench or corruption that warmer conditions keep concealed. In many places, heat is associated with decay: warmth releases smells, intensifies bodily presence, and brings human excess into the open. Here, however, the poem reverses that expectation. It is not heat but cold that reveals what lies beneath the surface. The frozen atmosphere uncovers a deeper moral, physical, or existential rottenness that had remained hidden.

The speaker contrasts this place with other cities where human excess is driven by heat. In those cities, warmth produces noise, appetite, sweat, crowds, and visible forms of deterioration. By comparison, this setting appears colder, quieter, and more restrained, yet it is not free from decay. Instead, corruption emerges differently. It is drawn out by cold rather than heat, suggesting a world where suffering is not flamboyant or overheated but bleak, numb, and persistent.

Cold is therefore portrayed as a destructive force. It does not merely chill the body; it damages identity, livelihood, and life itself. It maims people by stripping away their vitality, reducing them to survival, and forcing them into a diminished existence. The cold becomes almost violent, attacking the human capacity to act, work, hope, or define oneself. Under its pressure, people are not fully alive in any meaningful sense; they are worn down into endurance.

The poem also links figures such as Murphy, Molloy, and the Idiot Boy to this bleak existential landscape. These names evoke characters associated with retreat, helplessness, absurdity, and persistence in the face of meaninglessness. Their presence suggests a world in which human beings withdraw from ordinary social life and continue only through habit, inertia, or stubborn endurance. They are not heroic survivors but figures of reduced existence, moving through a hostile environment with little promise of renewal.

In the final lines, the poem presents human beings as “living corpses.” This image captures the poem’s darkest vision: people are alive biologically, but spiritually, socially, or emotionally they are already close to death. They barely live, yet they continue to exist until death finally overtakes them. The result is a bleak meditation on human endurance, in which life is stripped down to its bare minimum and survival itself becomes a kind of prolonged decay.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a bleak meditation on coldness, decay, and existential diminishment. Its repeated sensory imagery creates an atmosphere in which the physical world seems hostile, exhausted, and stripped of warmth. Cold is not merely a feature of the weather but a condition that affects the body, the mind, and the social environment. The urban setting reinforces this sense of desolation: streets, rooms, and public spaces appear drained of vitality, suggesting a world in which human beings survive without comfort, intimacy, or meaningful connection.

Within this environment, images of decay become central to the poem’s vision of human life. The emphasis on stench, bodily deterioration, and unpleasant sensory detail makes degradation impossible to ignore. Smell functions as a particularly powerful sign because it is invasive and inescapable; it reveals what sight might overlook or what society might prefer to conceal. The presence of stench therefore suggests both physical decline and moral or emotional abandonment. It marks figures who are still alive but who seem to exist close to a state of living death.

The poem’s allusions to Beckett-like figures deepen this atmosphere of bleak endurance. Like many of Beckett’s characters, the people in the poem appear reduced, withdrawn, and trapped in minimal forms of survival. They persist, but their persistence is grim rather than heroic. Retreat, silence, poverty, and bodily frailty become signs of a diminished existence in which life continues despite the absence of consolation or purpose. The poem does not romanticize suffering; instead, it presents survival as a bare, stubborn fact.

Ultimately, the poem suggests that human degradation becomes most visible under conditions of emotional and social coldness. When warmth, compassion, and communal care disappear, the body becomes the site where neglect is registered most clearly. Stench, then, is not only an image of decay but also a sign of endurance. It indicates that life remains, however damaged, exposed, and diminished. In this way, the poem transforms unpleasant sensory experience into a symbol of both human ruin and grim persistence.
outputs.L5:
**When the Unseal Happens**

When the moment finally arrives, the seal that once held everything closed begins to weaken. The silence breaks, and what was hidden beneath the surface slowly comes into view. The unseal is not always loud or dramatic; sometimes it is quiet, like the first breath after a long wait.

The act of unsealing can mean many things. It may reveal a secret, open a forgotten door, or release something that was kept safe for years. When the seal is broken, the past and present meet, and there is no way to return to what was before.

The unseal is a turning point. It invites discovery, but it also demands responsibility. What is opened must be understood, and what is revealed must be faced. In that moment, everything changes.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense modernist poem about Samuel Beckett’s fiction, using the recurring line “When it is cold it stinks” and references to Murphy, Molloy, and existential decay.
counterfactuals.output:
**When it is cold it stinks**

Murphy tied to his chair,  
star gone inward,  
mind’s little asylum clicking shut—  
a black sun among biscuits,  
ash in the mouth of God.

When it is cold it stinks.

Molloy on his bicycle of bones,  
sucking stones into order,  
then disorder,  
then the old arithmetic of loss;  
the road unspools like intestine,  
mother is a room,  
language a crutch,  
and every name limps.

When it is cold it stinks.

The body continues:  
that was the scandal.  
Knees, bowels, teeth,  
the skull’s damp chapel,  
a laugh left out overnight.  
Existence decays without drama,  
with clerical patience,  
with mud on its cuffs.

Murphy dreams the chessboard clean,  
Molloy forgets which leg is failing,  
Moran becomes the message he pursued—  
all of them reduced,  
refined,  
rotting toward a grammar of less.

When it is cold it stinks.

No tragedy now,  
only inventory:  
hat, stone, bicycle, bed,  
the sour rain of consciousness,  
the old imperative to go on  
spoiling in the jar.

And still the sentence crawls,  
blind worm,  
through the cold meat of meaning;  
still the voice, unburied,  
counts its own remains.

When it is cold it stinks.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a bleak literary pastiche in the style of W. H. Auden, treating cold weather as a metaphor for dehumanization in Beckett’s world.
counterfactuals.output:
**Cold Front over Beckett’s Country**

The barometer, impartial as a clerk,  
Fell through the night; by dawn the fields were white.  
No angels troubled them, no larks at work—  
Only the frost, arranging its polite  
And final signatures on gate and stone,  
As if to prove that nothing stands alone.

In huts where speech had learned to do without  
The costly human gestures of reply,  
Two figures nursed a boot, a rag, a doubt,  
And watched their little intimacies die.  
The stove gave out; the kettle would not sing.  
The rope hung limp, an undecided thing.

There was no winter once, or so they said,  
Only bad light, bad roads, a shabby tree;  
But cold came down and entered in the head,  
A civil servant of necessity.  
It numbered bones, it simplified the face,  
It made of every name an empty place.

The tramps, the sons, the masters in their bins,  
The mouth that poured its ashes through the dark,  
All felt the weather tightening their skins  
Till even suffering lost its private mark.  
Pain became public, hunger turned abstract;  
The heart was an administrative fact.

O little planet, shivering in its pose,  
How brave your ruined persons try to seem:  
One sucks a stone, one pares his ancient toes,  
One waits for orders in a stalled-out dream.  
They do not live; they merely still occur,  
Like snowflakes on a cancelled register.

And God, if there, kept warm behind a cloud,  
While Time, that punctual beggar, rubbed its hands.  
No trumpet spoke; no verdict was allowed;  
The cold outlived the laws of warmer lands.  
It asked no faith, accepted no excuse,  
And rendered every body into use.

So morning came, exacting and severe,  
With all the tenderness of iron tools.  
The ditch was hard, the blackened branches clear,  
The world instructed by its cleanest rules.  
A voice said, “Go.” Another answered, “Where?”  
The frost went on perfecting the air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a formal, allusive poem about a freezing city where bodies, names, and livelihoods are amputated by an inhuman gaze; include Beckettian references.
counterfactuals.output:
**The City Under the Eye**

In the white hour, when chimneys cease to pray,  
The city stiffens in its iron sleep;  
Frost nails the shutters shut, and far away  
The river drags a mirror through the deep.  

An eye without a lid, without a face,  
Looks down and measures breath against the snow;  
It has no rage, no pity, and no place—  
It only sees, and what it sees must go.  

First hands are taken: hands that stitched and shod,  
That warmed the bread, that signed a father’s name;  
Then tongues fall silent under glass and God,  
And every doorway gives its dead the same.  

The clerks are filed to ash, the porters thinned,  
The mothers counted out like frozen coins;  
A boy’s small shadow, halved by the wind,  
Crawls after him, but never quite rejoins.  

Names break like icicles from parish eaves;  
They splinter softly, neither heard nor missed.  
The ledgers bloom with blanks; the city grieves  
In ink so pale it hardly can exist.  

Here Hamm might sit enthroned in dust and rags,  
Blind to the dawn that never learns to rise;  
Here Clov might pace between the empty flags,  
Obeying exits barred by vacant eyes.  

And in some bin, where Nagg and Nell recall  
A kiss, a lake, a bicycle, a shore,  
The snow keeps falling with no end at all,  
As if the world had ended once before.  

O frozen trades, O amputated bread,  
O shops whose signs hang tongueless in the air—  
The gaze goes on subtracting from the dead  
What little death had had the grace to spare.  

No trumpet breaks the cold, no thaw begins;  
The sun, if sun it is, remains remote.  
We wait, like Vladimir with his ancient shins,  
For someone named but never known to note.  

Yet still, beneath the pavements’ blue-black stone,  
A pulse persists, diminutive and late:  
Not hope, perhaps—one cannot call it hope—  
But breath refusing to accommodate.  

And if the eye descends to make that cease,  
If night completes its inventory of harm,  
Still one lost name may gather in the freeze,  
A coal of speech concealed inside a palm.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem beginning with “When it is cold it stinks, and not till then,” exploring love, summer, canals, streets, and living corpses in a dark philosophical tone.
counterfactuals.output:
When it is cold it stinks, and not till then,  
the canal confesses what the summer hid:  
green throats of water, oil-slick, breath of fen,  
the drowned heat folded under every lid.  

We loved there once, beside the iron rail,  
where barges bruised the dusk with ropes and tar;  
your hand in mine felt temporary, frail,  
a match held up against a falling star.  

The streets were long, and shining after rain,  
each window kept a separate, hungry light;  
we spoke of joy as if it answered pain,  
as if a name could shelter us from night.  

But summer is the sweetest form of rot:  
it flowers over wounds, it gilds the bone;  
it teaches flesh to ripen and be caught  
between desire and being left alone.  

Now winter lifts the covers from the place.  
The canal exhales its doctrine: all things pass.  
The living corpses hurry, face by face,  
reflected briefly in the blackened glass.  

They move through streets that never learned to care,  
with hearts still beating like unpaid machines;  
each carries love’s old weather in the air,  
each wears a soul worn thin at all its seams.  

And I, no less cadaverous than they,  
still seek your shadow where the waters bend,  
as though the dead could bargain with decay,  
as though what stinks in cold might not be end.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a high-modernist critical-poetic response to Beckett’s Murphy and Molloy, with repeated variations on coldness, stench, and existential survival.
counterfactuals.output:
In *Murphy*, the room is cold because the mind wants it so: a little cell of negation, a chessboard of self-cancelling squares, a chair in which the body is bound not as punishment but as experiment. The cold is not weather. It is metaphysics entering by the joints. It is the chill of consciousness when it has dismissed the world and found, in the cleared space, not purity but a draught.

Murphy would survive by subtraction. Less world, less obligation, less noise from the broken apparatus of social life. He seeks the zero-degree of being: the mind rocking in its own black cradle, neither yes nor no, neither dead nor properly alive. But the body persists, inconveniently warm, and therefore humiliating. Hunger, sex, employment, the smell of others: all the old municipal stenches of existence return. Cold thought, warm flesh. Cold thought, foul air. Cold thought, and still the animal breathes.

And in *Molloy*, the cold has spread. It is no longer the clean cold of an inward chamber, but a roadside cold, ditch-cold, stone-cold, the cold of a body proceeding because it has forgotten how to stop. Molloy moves through a landscape of dwindling reasons. His bicycle is a theorem in decay; his sucking-stones are a liturgy of exhausted order. He survives not by triumph but by dwindling accurately. He endures by miscounting, by crawling, by refusing—if refusal is the word—to convert suffering into meaning.

Coldness again: not the heroic cold of mountain air, but the cold of knees, of fingers, of saliva, of language losing circulation. Beckett’s cold is anti-sublime. It does not elevate; it reduces. It does not clarify; it numbs. One thinks of the soul, if soul there be, as a badly wrapped parcel left at the wrong station.

Stench follows. The Beckettian universe does not merely appear; it smells. It smells of rooms unventilated, clothes unwashable, bodies that cannot escape their own evidence. Stench is the protest of matter against abstraction. Murphy may dream of pure mind, but the world answers with sweat, cabbage, hospitals, beds, breath. Molloy may speak in ruined sequences, but the body annotates the monologue with odour. The stink is democratic, intimate, irrefutable. It says: you are here. It says: you have been here too long. It says: thought is not a deodorant.

Coldness, stench, survival: Beckett arranges them not as symbols to be decoded, but as conditions to be undergone. The cold pares down illusion. The stench defeats transcendence. Survival remains, absurdly, after both have done their work.

Survival in *Murphy* is almost comic in its perversity: the desire not to live better, but to live less falsely, less externally, less under the tyranny of other people’s demands. Yet Murphy’s inward kingdom is a collapsing sovereignty. The self that retreats from the world discovers that it has imported the world’s disorder into itself. The mind is not a sanctuary; it is another asylum. The cold room is not outside history. It is history miniaturized, strapped to a chair.

Survival in *Molloy* is more ancient, more abject. It is the survival of the creature after the person has become uncertain. Name, destination, memory, mother, law: all are compromised. What remains is propulsion, however intermittent. A going on before the famous imperative has hardened into formula. Molloy survives by degrading the very idea of survival. He does not flourish; he continues. He does not overcome; he is not yet finished.

Coldness: the cold of the ditch, the cold of the institution, the cold of the sentence correcting itself into impotence.

Stench: the stench of flesh, the stench of narrative obliged to inhabit flesh, the stench of meaning rotting before it can become doctrine.

Survival: not salvation, not courage, not existentialist posture with collar turned up against the Paris wind, but the low mechanical miracle of not yet ceasing.

Beckett’s comedy is therefore glacial and fetid at once. A contradiction only to those who have not lived in the body. The laugh comes out white with cold; it comes out smelling of the grave and the lavatory. It is a laugh stripped of social polish, a laugh at the organism’s expense, a laugh that knows the skull is the last theatre and the mouth its broken proscenium.

In Murphy’s silence and Molloy’s prolixity there is the same ruined music: the mind seeking arrangements against chaos, then finding chaos within arrangement. Chess positions, sucking-stone permutations, journeys, interrogations, reports—these are systems built in the cold. They promise hygiene. They promise order. But stench seeps through the floorboards. The body spoils the diagram. The world re-enters by smell.

And still they go on, or fail to go on in ways indistinguishable from going on. Murphy inward, Molloy onward: two geometries of exhaustion. One contracts toward the sealed chamber, the other disperses across road, field, ditch, recollection. Both enact the modernist afterlife of the quest: no grail, no revelation, no homecoming, only the persistence of form after faith has leaked away.

Coldness is Beckett’s negative grace.

Stench is his incarnational truth.

Survival is his obscene benediction.

Not to be redeemed, not to be explained, not to be warmed by humanist embers: that is the dignity of these books. They do not console the creature. They stay with it. They sit beside it in the cold. They breathe its sour air. They watch it crawl, calculate, forget, resume. And from this nearly nothing—this chair, this road, this smell, this shiver—Beckett makes a literature of terminal continuance: the last elegance of the dispossessed body, the last metaphysics of bad weather, the last song sung through clenched teeth in a room that will not warm, in a world that will not sweeten, by a life that cannot quite consent to end.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
